body_markdown:
Nobody joins a car club for the cars.


This truth was very much on my mind after I spent several days with a tight-knit group of people who, for two decades, have bonded over their shared interest in Shelby Cobras and genuine admiration for each other, emphasis on the latter. The occasion was an annual Cobra rally organized by Tom Cotter and Jim Maxwell.[The article I wrote about their gathering](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/full-cobra-die-hard-shelby-owners-pile-on-miles/%E2%86%97) covers the cars, but I hope readers come away with an appreciation of what they started and what the rest of us can learn from their example.


Decades ago, when Cotter was looking to buy his first Cobra, he called Maxwell—known as a Cobra sage—for advice, which launched both their friendship and the annual rally. Cotter is the host of *[Barn Find Hunter](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7p8-TccjTk&list=PLHKCmmH-x9mLN0PNeFBtxyZ7olwptkO5q)* , a series that has run on Hagerty’s[YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@Hagerty) for over a decade. If you’ve watched the show, you know about his great cheer, his enthusiasm, and his curiosity.


What the show captures but perhaps doesn’t fully explain is a quality in Cotter that I find increasingly rare and increasingly valuable. It was crystallized for me by an unlikely source—the musical *Hamilton* . In one early scene, Aaron Burr offers the young Alexander Hamilton his personal philosophy in four words: *Talk less, smile more.*


Burr meant it cynically—as a strategy for political survival. But strip away the cynicism and what’s left is something worth practicing. In a world that rewards the loudest voice in the room, the people who ask questions and actually listen to the answers are a vanishing species. Cotter is one of them. He draws people out, he remembers what they told him last time, he asks the follow-up questions. He is sincerely interested in the answer.


Cars attract passionate people who like to talk about the things they love. That’s not a flaw—it’s what makes this community wonderful. But passion without curiosity is merely a monologue. The people who make these get-togethers memorable are usually the ones who came to learn something, not simply share what they already know.


What Cotter and Maxwell have built is a testament to that. Every year, they do the heavy lifting—the organizing, the logistics, all the invisible details that make an event feel effortless to everyone who shows up. And then they host with a generosity and selflessness that sets the tone for everything that follows. They are not the center of attention. They are the reason everyone else gets to be.


Cameron Neveu


If you’ve been reading Hagerty this year, you’ve noticed we’ve been beating a particular drum:[how to organize gatherings](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/how-to-organize-a-driving-rally-and-why-you-should/) , why they matter, and what they give back to the people who show up. I do it myself and I believe in it. Here is the thing about organizing: It is not hard. It does not require a venue or a budget or a committee. It requires one person willing to send the first email. Cotter and Maxwell did that 20 years ago, and look what grew from it.


That kind of hospitality is rarer than a numbers-matching Cobra. And like a numbers-matching Cobra, you know it immediately when you encounter it.


We could all stand to do a little more of it.
